title: I owe Villa the world but Man Utd are above them - Tielemans
description: Manchester United new boy Youri Tielemans gives his first extended interview on his £35m dream move, making it third time lucky for the ex-Aston Villa man.
fullText:
It was third time lucky this summer in the history of Youri Tielemans and Manchester United.

United looked seriously at the Belgium midfielder in 2019, after Tielemans had impressed in an initial loan spell at Leicester. And again in 2022, as they spent too long holding out for Frenkie de Jong to decide if he was prepared to leave Barcelona.

But it was this July, while the 29-year-old was on World Cup duty, when the Old Trafford outfit made their move, triggering a £35m release clause to snap Tielemans up on a five-year deal from Aston Villa.

"There had been two times that I spoke with the club, but it did not achieve anything," he recalled.

"I was very calm. I was not expecting much this summer, to be fair. I was just focused on my football, focused on the World Cup and trying to perform my best for my country.

"But you know every summer something can happen and obviously I was aware of the clause.

"I am very thankful to Aston Villa. I owe them the world. It is a great club, we did amazing things and they have put me back to my best level. But there are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them.

"It is a great achievement for any footballer to end up here. It means you have done well in your career. But it does not end there. I want to be successful."

Tielemans cameo against PSG hints at Man Utd future

Man Utd sign Tielemans for £35m from Aston Villa

Tielemans cuts a relaxed figure as he conducts his first extended media interview since his switch from Villa, taking time to personally shake hands with all the journalists present.

He positively beams at points, noticeably when he is asked whether – given he scored Leicester's winner in the 2021 FA Cup final and then the opener for Villa in their Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May – if he can bring goals to Manchester United.

It is also clear from his expression a partnership with skipper Bruno Fernandes is developing.

Senior Manchester United officials noticed it in Gothenburg last weekend, even though the pair were only on the pitch together for 26 minutes in the 1-1 draw with Paris St-Germain.

"It's really natural," he said. "He is a guy that can find space easily. I just try and find him so that he can move forward."

Tielemans is thoughtful though, and expansive in his answers, even if sometimes what he says is not quite what you expect to hear.

One of those is around the length of his career and the number of games he has played.

He made his professional debut for Anderlecht at 16. He has played 668 games for club and country and had to pull out of Belgium's World Cup quarter-final clash with Spain last month after experiencing an issue in the warm-up.

"I feel very good, actually," he said.

"In that last game, it was just an overload of too many games; too many minutes. Unfortunately, my body could not cope with it anymore.

"We played 120 minutes against Senegal, then played the US a few days later, three days after that we played against Spain.

"In the warm-up, my body just switched off for some reason.

"I do not think I am a player that absolutely needs a rest. Obviously, there are a lot of games, and the manager needs to manage the team, but when I am good, I am good.

"When it does not go well, I will know straight away and I will alert the manager. But it does not happen often."

While Tielemans is new to Manchester United, there are some familiar faces helping him to settle in.

Chief among them is Jonny Evans, a former team-mate at Leicester. The pair have remained close and Evans offered a positive character reference to head coach Michael Carrick.

Tielemans also played with Harry Maguire for a short period at Leicester, and Marcus Rashford was a team-mate at Aston Villa.

To the surprise of many, including himself probably, Rashford is back at his boyhood club, having initially left for Villa under a cloud after his fall-out with Ruben Amorim.

"He was great," said Tielemans.

"There had been so much talk about him, bringing pressure and the media around him, but he was so good.

"He was very humble and hard-working, and from the first training session you could tell his touch and acceleration was just amazing. That was what we needed at the time. He did many good things and hopefully he can bring them here."

It could be argued Tielemans' arrival addresses an issue Manchester United has had since Carrick quit in 2018; the scheming midfielder with an eye for a pass, who can break a defensive line.

In theory, it will allow Fernandes more room further forward and offer the opportunity to control games for a team that has, in recent times, tended to be viewed as being better on the counter-attack.

Tielemans had a brief chat with Carrick before he completed his move.

But the past 10 days have offered a great insight into Carrick's expectations.

"He wants me to be free on the pitch, to try and organise the team the best I can," he said.

"He has got his structure. He wants to have the ball and wants to press in certain ways.

"It might be different than what I am used to, but it is logical things in my opinion.

"It is just smelling football, which is what I have been doing from when I was young at Anderlecht, you know.

"For me, nothing changes, but it just needs to gel together."

title: Why is the women's 800m record so tough to break?
description: The world record for the women's 800m is the longest-standing in athletics. No-one has managed to break it for 43 years. Why?
fullText:
The world record for the women's 800m is the longest-standing in athletics. No-one has managed to break it for 43 years.

So why, despite leaps forward in shoe technology and our understanding of nutrition and recovery, has that record not fallen?

Great Britain's Keely Hodgkinson is one of the top three middle-distance runners in the world competing at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham this week. So could that record, finally, be broken?

The women's 800m world record is held by Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds in 1983.

There have been claims that Kratochvilova's performance in Munich was assisted by the systematic doping regime that existed in her country at the time - something she has strenuously denied.

Kratochvilova's record is not the only one to be questioned.

Marita Koch of East Germany set the women's 400m record two years later, in 1985 - when the country was known to be systematically doping its athletes.

But Koch never failed a drugs test, and always maintained she did nothing wrong.

In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005.

The proposals never went any further. But they sent a strong signal that some records set before 2005 - when World Athletics (formerly IAAF) started storing blood and urine samples - could be disputed.

Back in 1983, then 32-year-old Kratochvilova crossed the finish line more than seven seconds ahead of her closest rival, Poland's Jolanta Januchta.

No-one would come within a second of Kratochvilova's record for 25 years.

The closest any athlete has come to breaking it is Swiss athlete Audrey Werro, who ran a time of 1:53.80 in June this year.

Hodgkinson and gold medal rivals progress at Europeans

"Believe you me, that time of 1:53.28 is astonishing," Jenny Meadows, former British runner and coach to Hodgkinson, told BBC Sport.

"I won medals on a global level and I could not even comprehend that a female could run that sort of time."

But athletes have never been closer to breaking it.

Werro has twice gone under 1:54 this year, but still more than half a second from Kratochvilova's record.

Olympic champion Hodgkinson broke the 800m indoor record in February, which had stood since 2002, crossing the line in 1:54.87.

Then there's the Netherlands' Femke Broeders-Bol, still largely an unknown in the 800m after deciding to switch disciplines from 400m hurdles. But, with little 800m experience, she ran a time of 1:55.60 seconds at the Paris Diamond League event in June.

"They're all dragging each other to these incredible times. The level of the 800m has risen significantly in the past two years," said Jessica Ennis-Hill, who won heptathlon gold at the London 2012 Olympics.

Innovations in sports science have edged athletes closer too.

"Everyone is going faster than they used to be because the shoe technology is so much better," University of Exeter professor Andrew Jones told BBC Sport.

Jones specialises in applied physiology, working with middle and long-distance runners to chase faster times.

"We know more about various supplements, things like creatine, nitrate, but in particular bicarbonate.

"And we know more about what limits performance".

This includes our understanding of carbohydrates, and how to best fuel for a middle-distance race like the 800m.

"It's a bit like a Formula One race car," he added. "You want the car to cross the line almost empty of fuel. If you've got half a tank left, you've been weighing yourself down."

Now, in Birmingham, the best three 800m runners in the world are looking like they will contest a gripping final, if they come through Thursday's semi-finals. Whether that final will turn into a more tactical race or develop into a battle of speed remains to be seen.

"All it takes is one person to raise the bar and you think more things are possible," Hodgkinson told BBC Sport.

"Everyone knows that to keep up you have to keep getting better. It's a really exciting time for the women's 800m."

title: Zhang shocks Zhao in final-ball respot at China Open
description: Zhang Anda shocked world number three Zhao Xintong with a thrilling 6-5 victory by potting a respotted black ball in round one of the China Open.
fullText:
Zhang Anda shocked world number three Zhao Xintong with a thrilling 6-5 victory by potting a respotted black ball in round one of the China Open.

Zhang, who was down 3-0 in frames, fought back to eventually lead 5-4.

However, last year's world champion Zhao forced a deciding frame that ended in dramatic fashion.

"Today was just my day," Zhang said. "I hope that I can go far [in this tournament], I don't want them [two pots of the black] again. I was too nervous."

Zhang, ranked 19th in the world, was in control at 57-0 up, but Zhao fought back to lead with both players on the black.

The black was eventually potted by Zhang to force a respot - used as a tie-breaker when a frame ends with the scores level - with the 34-year-old prevailing.

He will now face England's Chris Wakelin.

"I made far too many mistakes today and I probably didn't deserve to win," Zhao added.

"I had prepared well for coming to Shanxi this time, and I didn't expect to lose in the first round. I played too badly and there was nothing I could do about it."

World number five John Higgins also lost in the first round after he was defeated 6-4 by 2015 world champion Stuart Bingham.
